Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Piblic Safety

Setting the Scene

Public safety refers to the protection of the general public, communities, and critical infrastructure from crimes, disasters, accidents, and other major threats through coordinated government and agency action.

Geospatial analytics, supported by multi-source geospatial data and geospatial data science and analysis methods, provides powerful means to transform location-based data into visual evidence, analytical insights, and decision support. It plays an important role in areas such as law enforcement, emergency management, disaster response, transportation safety, and environmental management.

A spatial point pattern represents a collection of geographic locations at which particular events occur, such as forest-fire detections or road traffic accidents. A spatio-temporal point pattern extends this representation by incorporating the time at which each event occurs, allowing analysts to investigate how the distribution and interaction of events vary across both space and time.

Understanding where and when public-safety events occur can help planners and managers identify areas of concern, understand patterns of event occurrence, allocate resources, and develop evidence-informed strategies for prevention and response.

Why Does Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Point-Pattern Analysis Matter?

Spatial and spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis can help to:

  • Identify spatial concentrations: Determine whether events are concentrated in particular areas rather than being distributed uniformly across the study area.
  • Understand temporal variation: Examine how event occurrence changes across days, months, seasons, or other relevant periods.
  • Investigate spatial interaction: Determine whether events exhibit evidence of clustering, inhibition, or approximate spatial randomness.
  • Identify emerging patterns: Examine whether the distribution or interaction of events changes over time.
  • Support resource allocation: Provide evidence that can inform the allocation of emergency services, prevention resources, infrastructure improvements, and other interventions.
  • Support planning and management: Translate spatial and spatio-temporal evidence into actionable insights for public-safety planning and management.

Importantly, an observed concentration of events should not automatically be interpreted as higher risk. The interpretation of event patterns should consider the study population, observation process, exposure, data quality, study window, and other relevant contextual factors.

Objectives

This take-home exercise investigates the spatial and/or spatio-temporal patterns of public-safety point events using one of the following case studies:

  • Forest-fire events in a selected regency of Kalimantan, Indonesia, during the available observation period in 2026; or
  • Road traffic accidents within the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area for the selected study year.

The specific objectives are:

  • To prepare and integrate real-world geospatial and temporal data for spatial and spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis.
  • To investigate first-order properties of the point pattern by examining how the intensity or distribution of events varies across space and/or time.
  • To investigate second-order properties by examining whether events exhibit evidence of spatial or spatio-temporal interaction, such as clustering, inhibition, or approximate randomness.
  • To critically evaluate the analytical assumptions, methodological choices, and limitations associated with the selected point-pattern methods.
  • To communicate the analytical findings effectively through appropriate geovisualisation and geocommunication.
  • To translate the analytical evidence into meaningful implications for public-safety planning and management.

The Data

Core Data

Option A: Forest-Fire Study

Use:

  • Forest-fire event data from the Fire Information for Resource Management System(FIRM).
  • Administrative boundary data for Indonesia from the appropriate Indonesia Geospatial data portal.

Kalimantan is a large geographic area comprising five provinces and numerous regencies. For this exercise, students should select one regency as the study area.

The analysis should use the fire-event observations available during the study period in 2026. Students should clearly state the observation period covered by their downloaded data.

Option B: Road Traffic Accident Study

Use one of the following datasets:

  • Thailand Road Accident Fatalities 2024, or
  • Thailand Road Accident [2019-2022].
Warning
  • The 2024 dataset is provided in Thai.
  • If the 2019–2022 dataset is used, students should restrict the analysis to 2022.

Use an appropriate administrative boundary dataset for Thailand, such as data from geoBoundaries.

Students selecting the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area should clearly define the geographic extent used as the study area and explain how the boundary was operationalised.

Additional Data

Students are free to incorporate additional datasets that can provide useful contextual information or support interpretation of the point patterns.

One recommended source is OpenStreetMap (OSM) data obtained through Geofabrik.

Additional datasets are not required. They should only be incorporated when they have a clear analytical or interpretive purpose.

The use of additional data does not automatically constitute Value-Added Analysis. What matters is whether the additional data contribute meaningful insight to the research question.

Study Design and Analytical Assumptions

Before conducting the point-pattern analysis, students must clearly define the analytical study design.

Your technical report must document:

Point Event Definition

Clearly define what constitutes a point event in your selected dataset.

Explain how you handle:

  • duplicate observations;
  • repeated observations or detections;
  • missing coordinates;
  • invalid coordinates or geometries;
  • observations outside the study area;
  • observations outside the selected temporal period; and
  • any other data-quality issues that may affect the point pattern.

Spatial Study Window

  • Clearly define the geographic area within which the point process is analysed.
  • Explain and justify the spatial boundary used.

Temporal Study Window

For spatio-temporal analysis, clearly define the period covered by the analysis and justify any temporal aggregation used.

Analytical Assumptions

For each major analytical method, explicitly state the assumptions underlying the method and discuss whether they are reasonable for your study.

Where an assumption may not hold, explain how this could affect the results and conclusions.

Methodological Decisions

Document and justify important analytical choices, including, where applicable:

  • coordinate reference system;
  • spatial or temporal aggregation;
  • bandwidth;
  • distance range;
  • temporal interval;
  • edge correction;
  • simulation settings;
  • reference or null model; and
  • other parameters that may materially affect the results.

The objective is not to eliminate all assumptions. The objective is to demonstrate that you understand them and recognise their implications.

The Tasks

Task 1: Data Preparation

Data Acquisition

Download the required core datasets from the data sources provided.

Document the source, date of access, geographic coverage, temporal coverage, and relevant characteristics of each dataset.

Data Wrangling and Quality Assessment

Prepare and tidy the datasets using appropriate R functions and packages.

Your data preparation should include, where appropriate:

  • data import;
  • data inspection;
  • data cleaning;
  • handling missing or invalid observations; coordinate and geometry validation;
  • coordinate reference system transformation; spatial filtering;
  • temporal filtering;
  • variable transformation or derivation;
  • integration of relevant spatial datasets; and
  • create spatial objects.

Document important data-quality problems and explain how they were addressed.

Task 2: First-Order Point-Pattern Analysis

Conduct appropriate first-order spatial and/or spatio-temporal point-pattern analyses using the prepared data.

Your analysis should investigate how the intensity or distribution of events varies across space and/or time.

You should:

  • select appropriate analytical methods; justify why the selected methods are appropriate;
  • explain important analytical parameters and assumptions;
  • produce appropriate statistical graphics and geovisualisations; and
  • interpret the resulting patterns in the context of your selected public-safety problem.
Warning

Simply producing a density map or statistical graphic without explaining the analytical reasoning behind it is insufficient.

Task 3: Second-Order Point-Pattern Analysis

Conduct appropriate second-order spatial and/or spatio-temporal point-pattern analyses to investigate the interaction among events.

Your analysis should examine whether the observed pattern provides evidence of phenomena such as:

  • clustering;
  • inhibition/regularity; or
  • approximate randomness.

For each major second-order analysis, you must:

  • State the research question being investigated.
  • Identify and justify the analytical method.
  • State the relevant assumptions.
  • Identify and justify the reference/null model against which the observed pattern is assessed.
  • Explain relevant analytical parameters and edge effects, where applicable.
  • Interpret the statistical results.
  • Discuss important limitations or caveats.
Tip

Remember that a pattern should not be labelled “clustered” merely because points appear visually concentrated on a map. The interpretation should be made relative to an appropriate analytical reference or null model.

Task 4: Integration and Interpretation

Integrate the findings from the first-order and second-order analyses.

Your discussion should address:

  • What does the first-order analysis reveal about event intensity or distribution?
  • What does the second-order analysis reveal about interaction among events?
  • How do the first-order and second-order findings complement each other?
  • Are the findings consistent across different analytical views?
  • What assumptions or limitations should be considered when interpreting the results?
  • Are there alternative explanations for the observed patterns?
Tip

Where appropriate, conduct a sensitivity or robustness analysis to determine whether important conclusions are sensitive to analytical choices such as bandwidth, distance range, temporal aggregation, or other parameters.

Task 5: Geovisualisation and Analytical Interpretation

Prepare appropriate geovisualisations and statistical graphics to communicate the findings.

For each major geovisualisation, provide a concise analytical interpretation of no more than 150 words.

The interpretation should explain:

  • what the visualisation reveals;
  • what evidence supports the interpretation; and
  • any important limitations or caveats.

The emphasis should be on analytical clarity and effective communication, rather than decorative or aesthetic complexity.

Task 6: Public-Safety Planning and Management

With reference to the analytical findings, discuss how the results could support public-safety planning and management.

Your discussion should be no more than 500 words.

Depending on the selected case study, relevant implications may include:

  • land-use planning;
  • transportation and road-safety planning;
  • emergency response;
  • infrastructure planning;
  • environmental management;
  • resource allocation;
  • risk mitigation; and
  • public-safety policy.
Important

Your discussion should distinguish between evidence supported directly by the analysis and interpretations or recommendations that require additional information.

Avoid making causal claims unless they are supported by appropriate evidence.

Grading Criteria

This exercise will be assessed using the following criteria:

Criteria Weights
Geospatial Data Wrangling and Data Quality 20%
Geospatial Point-Pattern Analysis and Statistical Reasoning 30%
Geovisualisation and Geocommunication 20%
Reproducibility and Analytical Documentation 15%
Bonus: Value-Added Analysis 15%
Total 100%

Geospatial Data Wrangling and Data Quality (20%)

You will be assessed on your ability to employ appropriate R functions and packages for modern geospatial data science to conduct the complete data-wrangling process.

This includes, but is not limited to:

  • data import;
  • data inspection;
  • data extraction;
  • data cleaning;
  • spatial transformation;
  • temporal transformation;
  • geometry validation;
  • variable derivation;
  • integration of datasets; and
  • spatial objects creastion

Particular attention will be given to your ability to identify and appropriately address data-quality issues that could affect the subsequent analysis.

Warning

Real-world geospatial data rarely arrive analysis-ready. Missing values, duplicate records, invalid geometries, inconsistent coordinate systems, inaccurate locations and other data-quality problems may affect your results. Your responsibility is to identify, diagnose and appropriately address these issues before conducting the analysis.

Geospatial Analysis and Statistical Reasoning (30%)

You will be assessed on your ability to:

  • correctly apply appropriate first-order and second-order point-pattern methods;
  • distinguish between first-order and second-order properties;
  • formulate appropriate analytical questions;
  • justify methodological choices;
  • state and evaluate relevant assumptions;
  • identify and justify appropriate reference/null models;
  • interpret statistical results correctly;
  • evaluate limitations and uncertainty; and
  • integrate evidence from multiple analytical approaches.

What does “excellent geospatial analysis” mean?

An excellent submission does not simply demonstrate that you can run R functions and produce maps or statistical graphics. It demonstrates that you can think analytically.

You should be able to explain:

  • What? — What pattern does the analysis reveal?
  • Why? — Why is this method appropriate?
  • Assumptions? — Under what assumptions should the result be interpreted?
  • Compared with what? — What reference or null model provides the basis for assessing the pattern?
  • So what? — Why does the finding matter for the public-safety problem?
  • How certain? — What limitations or alternative explanations should be considered?
  • Can others reproduce it? — Could another analyst understand and reproduce your workflow?
Tip

The emphasis is on analytical reasoning, not merely obtaining numerical or graphical output from R.

Geovisualisation and Geocommunication (20%)

You will be assessed on your ability to communicate complex geospatial findings through effective visual representations.

Assessment will consider:

  • analytical accuracy;
  • appropriate choice of visualisation;
  • spatial and temporal clarity;
  • effective visual encoding;
  • readability;
  • integration of statistical and cartographic evidence;
  • ability to highlight meaningful patterns; and quality of analytical interpretation.
Tip

Visual attractiveness alone will not constitute effective geovisualisation.

Reproducibility and Analytical Documentation (15%)

Reproducibility is a key learning outcome of this course.

Your Quarto technical report should document sufficient information for another analyst to understand and reproduce your analytical workflow.

This includes:

  • data sources and acquisition;
  • data-preparation procedures;
  • data-quality decisions;
  • analytical methods;
  • analytical parameters;
  • assumptions;
  • reference/null models;
  • R packages and functions;
  • code;
  • outputs; and
  • interpretation of the analytical procedures.
Tip

Simply providing code chunks is insufficient. You must explain the purpose of each major analytical step, the function(s) used, the reason for the analytical decision, and any assumptions or limitations involved.

Bonus: Value-Added Analysis (15%)

Students are encouraged to explore beyond the core methods covered in class.

Students may extend their analysis using an appropriate geospatial analytical method not covered in the core exercise.

A qualifying value-added analysis should:

  • address a meaningful analytical question;
  • be geospatial in nature;
  • be methodologically appropriate;
  • be clearly justified;
  • identify relevant assumptions and limitations; and
  • provide substantive additional insight.
Note

Simply applying an additional method or producing an additional visualisation without demonstrating its analytical contribution will not qualify for bonus marks.

Examples may include, but are not limited to, an alternative spatial-statistical approach, advanced spatio-temporal analysis, simulation-based analysis, or another appropriately justified geospatial method.

The bonus is intended to reward meaningful analytical exploration, not prior knowledge of advanced software or techniques.

Qualitative grading rubric of Value-Added Analysis

Level Descriptor
Exceptional Contribution Introduces a well-chosen geospatial analytical approach beyond the core scope that addresses a meaningful additional question and generates substantive new insight. The method is appropriately justified, implemented and interpreted, with assumptions and limitations clearly considered.
Meaningful Contribution Extends the analysis using an appropriate additional geospatial method and provides useful additional insight. The method and findings are reasonably justified and interpreted.
Limited / No Bonus The extension adds limited analytical value, lacks sufficient methodological justification, or mainly duplicates the core analysis. No bonus is awarded where the additional method does not provide meaningful new insight.
Important

Value-Added Analysis is not awarded for simply using a more advanced R package, producing additional visualisations, or applying a method that was not covered in class. Bonus credit is awarded for demonstrating meaningful additional analytical insight through an appropriately justified geospatial approach.

Submission Requirements

Executive Summary

Prepare an Executive Summary of no more than 10 slides, excluding the cover page and content page.

The Executive Summary must be prepared using Quarto revealjs.

The presentation should communicate the essential:

  • research question;
  • study area and data;
  • analytical approach;
  • key findings;
  • important visual evidence;
  • limitations; and
  • public-safety implications.

You are required to publish the Executive Summary on Vercel or another appropriate web-hosting service.

Technical Report

Prepare a comprehensive Technical Report using Quarto in HTML format.

The Technical Report should provide sufficient detail to document and reproduce the complete analytical workflow.

It should include, where appropriate:

  • Introduction and study context
  • Research question and objectives
  • Data and study design
  • Data preparation and quality assessment
  • Analytical assumptions and methodological decisions
  • First-order Spatial Point Patterns analysis
  • Second-order Spatial Point Patterns analysis
  • Integrated findings and discussion
  • Geovisualisation and geocommunication
  • Public-safety planning and management implications
  • Limitations
  • References

You are required to publish the Technical Report on Vercel or another appropriate web-hosting service.

Quarto Project and Reproducibility

The complete Quarto project for the take-home exercise must be pushed to your GitHub repository.

The repository should contain the necessary files to demonstrate the reproducibility of your analysis, subject to any data-licensing or redistribution restrictions.

Submission Links

Update Take-home Exercise 1 links to the:

  • Executive Summary;
  • Technical Report; and
  • GitHub repository

on the coursework website and provide the required links through eLearn.

Due Date

27th September 2026 (Sunday), 11.59pm (midnight).

References

Peer Learning

Students are encouraged to consult appropriate academic references, official data documentation, package documentation, and other credible sources when conducting the analysis.

Peer learning and discussion are encouraged. However, the submitted analysis, interpretation, code, visualisations and technical report must represent your own work.

Where external sources, code, analytical methods, or ideas have materially informed your work, they should be appropriately acknowledged and referenced.

AI Tools: Responsible Use and Learning Policy

AI tools, including generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and similar applications, are increasingly becoming part of professional data analytics practice. The purpose of this exercise is not to prohibit the use of AI tools, but to ensure that their use supports learning rather than substitutes for your own analytical thinking and judgement.

You are responsible for all analysis, interpretation, conclusions, code and visualisations submitted for this exercise.

1. Acceptable Use of AI Tools

You may use AI tools for purposes that support your learning and communication, including:

  • improving the clarity, grammar and readability of your writing;
  • improving the structure and organisation of a draft technical report;
  • identifying unclear or ambiguous expressions in your own writing;
  • obtaining general explanations of statistical or geospatial concepts that you are trying to understand;
  • brainstorming possible questions or analytical perspectives before conducting your own analysis; and
  • assisting with language expression, particularly where English is not your first language.

For example, after completing your own technical report, you may use an AI tool to improve the clarity and quality of the English. However, the analytical content, findings, interpretation and conclusions must originate from your own work.

2. Use of AI Tools That Is Not Permitted

You must not use AI tools as a substitute for performing or understanding the analysis yourself.

In particular, you must not:

  • ask an AI tool to provide a direct code chunk that performs a specific analytical task required in this exercise, and then use that code as your own analytical solution;
  • provide your analysis output, statistical results, maps or graphs to an AI tool and ask it to interpret the results or write the interpretation for you;
  • ask an AI tool to determine what statistical or geospatial method should be used and then adopt its recommendation without independently understanding and justifying the method;
  • ask an AI tool to generate the analytical findings, discussion, conclusions or planning implications of your study;
  • submit AI-generated analytical reasoning or interpretation as your own work; or
  • use AI-generated content that you cannot explain or defend.

The key principle is:

AI may help you learn and communicate, but it must not do the analytical thinking for you.

3. A Simple Test

Before using an AI-generated response in your work, ask yourself:

“Could I explain and defend this analysis, code, interpretation or conclusion to my instructor without relying on the AI tool?”

If the answer is no, you should not use it in your submission.

You should be able to explain:

  • what you did;
  • why you did it;
  • how the method works;
  • what assumptions it makes;
  • what the results mean;
  • what the limitations are; and
  • why your conclusions are supported by the evidence.

4. AI and Your Technical Report

The technical report must represent your own analytical work and judgement.

Using AI to improve the language of a completed draft is acceptable. However, students should not use AI to generate the substantive analytical sections of the report, including:

  • methodological decisions;
  • assumptions;
  • statistical interpretation;
  • findings;
  • discussion;
  • conclusions; and
  • recommendations.

In other words:

Write the analysis yourself first. Use AI, if needed, to help communicate your analysis more clearly but not to create the analysis for you.

5. Verification and Accuracy

AI tools can produce inaccurate, incomplete or inappropriate information.

If you use AI for learning or language assistance, you remain responsible for verifying the accuracy of the information and for ensuring that your submitted work reflects your actual analysis.

Do not assume that an AI-generated explanation, R function, statistical interpretation or methodological recommendation is correct simply because it appears plausible.

6. Transparency

If AI tools are used substantially in preparing your submission, briefly disclose their use in the Technical Report.

For example:

Note

AI Use Declaration: Generative AI was used to improve the English language, grammar and clarity of the technical report after completion of the student’s own analysis. No AI-generated code, analytical interpretation or conclusions were used in the submitted work.

Students who use AI for other permitted learning purposes should describe the purpose briefly.
